# rodzaj: greet (barman), wench (kelnerka), music (grajkowie), sit (bywalec zaprasza), table (scenka: kwestie rozdzielone " || ")
# region: any north iron west reach river vale storm crown dorne essos | temat: general war peace winter

column4: Welcome to {INN}. Ale, bread, a bench by the fire - what'll it be?
Shut the door behind you, the draught eats my fire. Now, what can I pour you?
Coin first, talk after. That's the rule in {INN}. What are you drinking?
Mind your sword in here. We've had soldiers through all week and I'm short two stools already.
Come in out of the cold. There's mulled ale on the hearth, if you've the coin.
Stamp the snow off your boots. Ale's brown, the stew's hot, and nobody asks your business.
Sit where you like, only not by the old man at the fire. That's been his seat since before the last winter.
Winter's teeth are out tonight. A cup of something hot, friend?
Salt on your cloak and coin in your fist, I hope. What will it be?
Good day to you. The wine comes up from the Reach, the ale is our own. Which will you have?
Welcome, welcome. Summerwine or ale - we have the one in plenty and the other in better plenty.
Another traveller on the road. Sit, eat, keep your head down - these days that's the best advice in the riverlands.
If you've come to burn us out, you're late, someone did it last spring. If you've come to drink, sit down.
You've come down from the high road? Then you've earned a cup. What'll it be?
Hang your cloak by the fire, the storms will have soaked you through. Ale or something stronger?
Fresh from the city or bound for it? Either way, you'll want a drink.
Out of the sun, friend. Our wine is red and strong, and the shade is free.
Come, come, sit. Wine from three cities and tales from nine. What will you have?
Ale's at the counter, love. Ask the keeper - he counts every drop.
Mind the floor, it's wet. Someone's always spilling something in here.
If you want a bed, it's the keeper you want. If you want gossip, it's the drovers by the fire.
Three lots of soldiers this month, and not one of them paid for their own cup.
Keep your hands to yourself and your boots near the fire, and we'll get on fine.
Don't sit by the window. Things come through windows these days.
You look thirsty. Everyone who comes in off that road looks thirsty.
The keeper says I'm to smile at every traveller. There. Now go and pay him.
We play for the room. A coin in the cup keeps the strings in tune.
A request? We know a dozen songs, and half of them are even decent.
Hush now, we're between songs. The next one is sad, so drink first.
We've a song about a winter that lasted a lifetime. It goes on a bit, like the winter.
We don't sing the war songs here. Folk have heard enough of the real thing.
A love song, a drinking song or a song about a knight? We do all three at once, if you pay double.
Pull up a stool, friend. We were just putting the world to rights.
Sit, sit. There's room if Wat moves his elbows.
A new face! Sit down and tell us nothing - we'll do the talking.
Shove up, lads, let the traveller near the fire.
Join us. In this heat a man shouldn't drink alone.
Sit, sit, and do not mind our tongues - we argue about everything.
Now that's a friend! Your health, stranger.
Gods bless an open purse. Drink, lads!
To the road, and to whoever pays for it!
To warm hearths and short winters.
To the sun, and to a guest who knows his manners.
Roads are worse every year. || Roads? It's the tolls I mind. Every bridge has a lord's man on it now. || And every lord's man has a hand out. || Drink up. Talking won't mend either.

My cousin swears he saw a two-headed calf at the last market. || Your cousin swears he saw a lot of things after his third cup. || He did say it was a small calf. || Then it's settled. Small calf, two heads, one cousin too many.
Price of salt went up again. || Everything's gone up but the price of a man's work. || My grandfather said the same. || Then your grandfather was right too.
Who's the stranger? || Paying customer, by the look of the purse. || Then he's no stranger. Sit, sit.
They say the keeper waters the ale. || The keeper says he waters the floor and the ale finds its own way. || Either way it's wet and it's cheap. || Cheap is the only thing anybody can afford.
I've a mule that knows the road better than I do. || Then why don't you send the mule to market and stay home? || Because the mule doesn't haggle. || Neither do you, from what I've seen.
Soldiers came through again last week. Took two pigs and a cart. || Did they pay? || One of them said thank you. That's something. || That's more than the last lot.
Which side are we on this month? || The side of whoever is standing in the village with a spear. || That's no side at all. || It's the only one that ever wins round here.
My boy was taken for the levy. || Mine too, two harvests back. He came home. || Whole? || Most of him. He laughs less.
Quiet on the roads this season. || Too quiet. Quiet means someone's planning something. || Or it means folk are tired of fighting. || I'll believe that when the lords do.
Snow's early. || Snow's always early to the man with no firewood. || I've got firewood. || Then you'll be getting visitors.
My well froze last night. || So did my wife's temper. || The well thaws by noon at least. || Aye. You've the better bargain there.
The old woman down the track says the winter will be long. || She says that every year. || And every year it's long. || Fine. Next year I'll listen to her.
A man came through from the hills, said he heard drums at night. || Drums or his own head? || He'd been drinking, if that's what you're asking. || That's the only way anyone hears drums up there.
Stew's thin tonight. || The stew is honest. It's the winter that's thin. || Then we'll eat honest and be cold. || Same as always.
My brother went reaving and came back with a bell. || A bell? What use is a bell? || He says it's worth more than the silver. || Then he was robbed by the men he robbed.
The miners up the valley are paid in coin again. || Gold coin? || Copper. Gold stays where it's dug. || As it always does.
Best harvest in years, and the price fell through the floor. || That's how it goes. Too much is as bad as too little. || Not for the man buying. || The man buying never ploughs.
A knight passed through, looking for a tourney. || Did he find one? || He found the keeper's daughter. || Then he found a tourney after all.
Fields by the ford flooded again. || They flood every spring. || Not like this. The water came right to the doors. || Then build higher, or pray harder.
Burned out three farms down by the lake, they did. || Who? || Does it matter? Banners change. Fire doesn't. || Pour another. I don't want to think about it.
My neighbour hid his grain under the floor. || Smart man. || Not smart enough - the soldiers burned the floor. || Then he's warm, at least, for a while.
The road down from the mountains is closed again. || Rockfall? || Clansmen. They take a toll in sheep. || Better sheep than heads.
Lost half the roof in the last storm. || Only half? You're lucky. || The other half landed on my brother's barn. || Then he's the lucky one. Two roofs.
The city's full of people and empty of bread. || Then why does everyone go there? || Because the bread there is the only bread there is. || Or because they think it is.
The water seller raised his prices again. || In this heat he can charge what he likes. || He'll charge it once too often. || Then we'll drink wine like sensible folk.
The galley from the east brought silk and fever. || Which sold faster? || The fever. It's free. || Then the silk merchant's ruined.
A sellsword was here last night, offering his sword to anyone. || Any takers? || Only the keeper, to pay his tab. || A man of many uses, then.
